reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A port-wine stain is a capillary (vascular) malformation present at birth that, unlike an infantile haemangioma, does not proliferate and does not spontaneously resolve
It appears as a flat, sharply demarcated pink to red patch that often follows a segmental or dermatomal distribution and tends to darken and thicken with age
Over decades some lesions develop cobblestoning, nodularity, and soft-tissue or bony overgrowth of the affected area
A facial stain involving the ophthalmic (forehead and upper eyelid) distribution raises concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome, with associated leptomeningeal vascular malformation and glaucoma
Any child with a periocular or ophthalmic-distribution stain needs ophthalmological assessment for glaucoma and appropriate neurological evaluation
Extensive limb capillary malformations can be a feature of overgrowth syndromes, so assess for limb asymmetry and hypertrophy
Pulsed-dye laser is the mainstay of treatment and works best when started early, though multiple sessions are needed and complete clearance is not guaranteed
The visible facial lesion carries a significant psychosocial burden, and support and camouflage advice are an important part of holistic care
reference.pathophysiology: A port-wine stain results from a developmental malformation of the superficial dermal capillaries and postcapillary venules, which are abnormally dilated and increase in ectasia over time. Many cases are associated with somatic activating mutations in genes of the GNAQ/GNA11 pathway, arising during embryogenesis and affecting a clone of vascular and surrounding cells. Because the abnormality is structural rather than proliferative, the number of vessels is essentially fixed, but progressive vascular dilatation and, in some cases, associated soft-tissue overgrowth account for the darkening and thickening seen with age. The same mosaic mutations underlie the neurological and ocular features when the malformation extends beyond the skin.
additionalDifferentials: Infantile haemangioma (proliferates then involutes, unlike a port-wine stain)
Naevus simplex / salmon patch (transient, midline, fades)
Other capillary malformations within overgrowth syndromes
Angioma serpiginosum and other acquired vascular patches
Reticulate vascular patterns such as cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on a congenital, non-involuting, well-demarcated vascular patch
Ophthalmological review for glaucoma with ophthalmic-distribution facial lesions
Brain MRI to assess for leptomeningeal involvement when Sturge-Weber syndrome is suspected
Assessment for limb overgrowth and, if indicated, imaging for associated vascular or overgrowth syndromes
Genetic evaluation in syndromic or extensive presentations where appropriate
redFlags: Ophthalmic-distribution facial stain raising concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome, seizures, and developmental effects
Signs of glaucoma such as a large or cloudy eye, tearing, or photophobia requiring urgent ophthalmology input
Progressive soft-tissue or skeletal overgrowth of the affected region
Extensive limb capillary malformation with asymmetry suggesting an overgrowth syndrome
New nodularity, bleeding, or ulceration within a long-standing lesion prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: A port-wine stain is a lifelong lesion that persists and typically darkens and thickens over time; the skin lesion itself is benign, but associated syndromic features determine broader outcome, and laser treatment can substantially lighten many lesions though results vary and maintenance may be required.
pitfalls: Confusing it with an infantile haemangioma and wrongly reassuring parents it will disappear
Missing the association with Sturge-Weber syndrome in an ophthalmic-distribution facial lesion
Failing to arrange glaucoma screening in at-risk infants
Overlooking limb overgrowth syndromes in extensive capillary malformations
Neglecting the psychological impact and the value of early laser referral
management: Pulsed-dye laser therapy as the mainstay to lighten the malformation, begun early and repeated as maintenance since lesions persist and darken over time
Ophthalmological review for glaucoma in any lesion involving the ophthalmic distribution, with pressure-lowering treatment as required
Brain MRI and neurology referral when Sturge-Weber syndrome is suspected, with anticonvulsant therapy for associated seizures
Assessment for limb asymmetry and soft-tissue or bony overgrowth, with orthopaedic and vascular input where an overgrowth syndrome is identified
Psychological support and skin camouflage for the cosmetic and social impact of a visible facial lesion
Genetic evaluation in syndromic or extensive presentations where appropriate
